- Confirm the removal. The Remove property window lists what happens next: the property leaves Fabrica, you authorize and sign the deed, and the county records it. You check one box confirming that this permanently removes the property from Fabrica and that you still need to authorize the deed transfer, sign the deed and complete county recording, then click Remove property. When it completes you will see "Property removed", and we will email you the next steps toward signing the deed.

- Authorize the deed transfer. On the property page, click Sign authorization and approve the Authorize deed transfer request in your account. Only the account that held the property's token can do this step.

- Sign the deed with an online notary. The session takes about 10 minutes. Have your ID ready.

- County recording. We send the signed deed to the county recorder. When it comes back stamped, we email you the recorded deed and your trust agreement. The property is now in your name.

passages.title: How do I remove my property from Fabrica?
passages.text:
Recording usually takes days, depending on the county. If you change your mind early in the process, you can cancel; you will be asked to confirm with Yes, Cancel Offramp.

Two notes about the recorded deed:

- It is emailed to the person who signed the removal documents. If a co-owner or a company signer completed the notary session, they are the one who receives it.

- You can always verify the recording independently with the county recorder's office; the deed is a public record. If you retired the token but never received a recorded deed, contact us in the chat right away so we can check where the paperwork stands.

passages.title: How do I remove my property from Fabrica?
passages.text: There is no Fabrica fee to remove a property. Counties charge their own recording costs, and Fabrica guides you through them as part of the process.

passages.title: How do I remove my property from Fabrica?
passages.text:
Your independence is built in. The token lives on Ethereum, a public network, so you can retire ("burn") it yourself using a public tool like Etherscan, without touching the Fabrica website. Our system detects the burn and starts the deed paperwork automatically. The trust agreement is open source, and because it holds record title at the county, a real-estate lawyer could complete the deed transfer even if Fabrica were gone. Your ownership never depends on our website staying up.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Off-ramp (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/off-ramp)

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.sectionTitle: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.text: Not every property is listed for sale, and not every listed price is the one you want to pay. You can send the owner an offer directly from the property page.

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.text:
Offers are made in USDC, a stablecoin (a digital dollar). You need enough USDC in your account to cover your offer amount, so that if the owner accepts, the sale can settle right away. There is no extra fee for making an offer.

If you signed up with email and pay by bank, you won't have USDC sitting in your account. On a listed property, the simpler path is Buy now, which takes bank and card payments directly. If you want to make an offer instead, message us through the chat bubble and we will help you get your account funded first.

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.text:
- On the property page, find the Marketplace card and click Send offer. The button is there whether or not the property is listed for sale. The Place an offer window opens.

- Enter your Offer Amount (USD).

- Set Offer Valid For: anywhere from 1 to 60 days. After that window, the offer expires on its own.

- Complete the two quick steps the app walks you through: Allow the offer amount (as the app says, this "lets the seller collect USDC from your account if they accept your offer") and Sign your offer. When you see "Great news: your offer is live!", the owner has it.

The owner is notified. If they accept before the offer expires, the sale settles automatically: they get paid and you become the owner, in the same transaction. You will get a confirmation email.

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.sectionTitle: Can I talk to the owner first?
passages.text: Usually the offer is the conversation. There is no general messaging between buyers and owners on Fabrica. Some property pages and owner profiles show a Message button next to the owner's name when the owner has chosen to accept messages; if you see it, you can use it. Your email address is shared with the owner so they can reply directly. Otherwise, sending an offer is the reliable way to start: the owner sees your offer with your terms, and accepting it is their answer.

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.text: You can withdraw an active offer at any time before it is accepted. On the property page, the offers list shows yours as "Your offer" with a Withdraw button. The window that opens is titled Cancel offer; confirm it and you'll see "Your offer is canceled", meaning the seller can no longer accept it. If the offer simply expires, you don't need to do anything.

passages.title: How do I make an offer on a property?
passages.text:
Some property pages show Unclaimed. That means the owner hasn't finished setting the property up on Fabrica yet. You can still send an offer, and it may nudge them to finish, but they cannot accept it until the property is fully set up.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more:

- Trading on Fabrica (developer docs) (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/trading)

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.sectionTitle: What happens when your property sells
passages.text: Congratulations, you sold your land. Here's what happens to your money, and what paperwork follows.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.text:
There is no escrow on Fabrica. The buyer becomes the owner and you get paid in the same transaction.

- If the buyer paid with the funds in their Fabrica account or by card, your proceeds arrive in your account right away as stablecoins (digital dollars).

- If the buyer paid by bank transfer, the sale completes once the payment clears. Your property page shows Sale pending with "You'll get paid by" and the expected date, and we'll email you when the money lands.

- If the buyer paid by wire, the sale completes once the wire arrives, and your proceeds arrive in your account then.

Your proceeds are the sale price minus Fabrica's fee. Fabrica charges 1% of the sale price, paid from the seller's proceeds. The buyer pays exactly the listed price. So a $100,000 sale puts $99,000 in your account.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.sectionTitle: Moving the money to your bank
passages.text:
Open your profile and click Cash out next to your balance. The Cash out window asks for three things:

- The amount. Your available balance is shown beside it, with a Max shortcut. The smallest cash out is $5.

- To: the bank the money goes to. The first time, the window says "Two quick things before your first cash out.": you verify your identity once (a short form checked by Coinflow, our payment provider) and connect a bank in your name for payouts. After that, your banks are listed, and Add a bank connects another.

- Speed: the options are named by how fast they arrive, such as Fastest, 1 business day, 3 business days or, for larger amounts, Wire. Each one shows the amount that arrives, the fee or "No fee", and "Expected by" with a date. Speeds that can't take your amount are hidden.

Click Review, check the amount, fee and destination, then click Cash out $X and approve the request once in your account. You'll see "Cash out on its way", and we email you when the money arrives. If a cash out can't be completed, the money comes back to your account.

A few things to know:

- Fabrica does not add a withdrawal fee. The fee shown belongs to the payment processor, and you see the exact amount you will receive before you confirm.

- Each speed has its own limit. For a large amount, pick a speed that accepts it, or split it into more than one cash out.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.text: Usually nothing needs to change at the county when your property sells. Some counties ask to be notified of the change of ownership, and we file that paperwork for you. If extra information is needed, we may email you (subject: "Action Required: Transfer Paperwork"). Just reply or follow the steps in the email.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.sectionTitle: When your buyer pays by bank
passages.text: Not every sale settles right away. If your buyer pays by bank transfer, the sale completes once their payment clears, usually by the expected date the app shows. During that window the property is still yours: the page says the token is still yours until the buyer's bank clears the payment, and then it moves to them, and the property with it. Buying and offers are paused on the property while the sale is pending. We email you when the money is on its way and again when you have been paid. If the buyer's payment fails or is returned, we will let you know and your property stays with you. There is nothing you need to do while a bank payment clears.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.sectionTitle: If the county still bills you after a sale
passages.text: If a tax bill or notice for land you already sold shows up in your name, nothing is wrong with the sale. The county most likely still has your details from before you added the property to Fabrica. Forward it to us through the chat and we will sort it out.

passages.title: What happens when your property sells
passages.text:
We can't give tax advice, but here's what to know:

- Income and capital gains. If you sold for more than you paid, you may owe tax on the gain. Real estate sales are generally reported to the IRS on Form 1099-S. Talk to a tax professional about your situation.

- Property taxes. Once the sale completes, responsibility for property taxes passes to the buyer along with ownership.

- No pro-rata tax settlement. There is no escrow or closing settlement on Fabrica, so property taxes are not prorated between buyer and seller. If you prepaid taxes for the year, the sale does not refund the surplus. The price shown on Fabrica is final and inclusive of all sale terms, so set your price with that in mind.

- No withholding. Fabrica does not withhold state or federal taxes from your sale proceeds. Some states have their own withholding or filing rules, especially for sellers who live out of state. Ask a tax professional what applies to you.

One more thing: sales on Fabrica are final. Once the transaction completes, it can't be reversed.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Selling (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/selling) and fees (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/fees) in our docs.

passages.title: Lending on Fabrica: how it works
passages.sectionTitle: Lending on Fabrica: how it works
passages.text: You can fund land-backed loans on Fabrica. Pool deposits are available in the app for signed-in users holding USDC. Bank funding is not yet available. Email hello@fabrica.land or open the chat bubble in the corner if you want to talk it through first. Here is the model in plain terms.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Lending on Fabrica: how it works
passages.text:
Landowners on Fabrica borrow against their properties through a DeFi lending pool. A pool is a shared fund with its own automated rules: depositors put in USDC, a stablecoin (a digital dollar), and the pool lends it out against tokenized properties. Borrowers pay interest, and that interest goes to the pool's depositors. Fabrica is the platform, not the lender.

Every property backing a loan has been through Fabrica's onboarding: the deed sits in a recorded trust, title has been checked, fees must be in good standing, and property taxes must be verifiably current before the pool will lend. Loans are conservative by design, sized against the minimum of two independent valuation models.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Lending on Fabrica: how it works
passages.text: Land is one of the oldest forms of collateral there is. What Fabrica adds is speed and enforceability: loans are funded and settled onchain without a traditional closing, collateral custody is handled automatically by the pool, and if a borrower defaults there is a defined legal path to recovery (see "What happens when a loan defaults?" (https://help.fabrica.land/en/articles/8673843-i-m-a-lender-and-i-received-a-token-from-a-defaulted-loan-what-do-i-do-with-it) in this collection). This is a new way to access an old asset class. As with any lending, capital is at risk, and you should do your own diligence.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Lending on Fabrica: how it works
passages.text:
Sign in to the app with a wallet holding USDC and deposit into a pool. Bank funding is not yet available. If you want to talk it through first, email hello@fabrica.land or open the chat bubble in the corner, and we will walk you through current options and requirements.

Learn more: For capital providers (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/for-capital-providers) · How the lending pool works (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/lending-pool) · Lending guide (https://blog.fabrica.land/lending-guide)
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Who is the lender?
passages.text:
Your loan does not come from Fabrica, and it does not come from a person reviewing your file. It comes from a DeFi lending pool.

A DeFi lending pool is a shared fund that runs on its own rules, on open software rather than at a bank (DeFi is short for decentralized finance). People and institutions deposit stablecoins (digital dollars) into the pool, and the pool lends that money out against properties like yours, automatically. The depositors earn the interest borrowers pay; that is why they fund the pool.

Because the pool is autonomous, there is no negotiation and nobody to persuade. The Amount, Duration, interest rate ("Interest at X% APR") and You repay by figures you see on the Instant Liquidity card come from the pool's own math: how much money it currently holds, its offered terms, and a conservative valuation of your property. Rates move with pool conditions, so the same property can see different offers on different days.

Fabrica's role is the platform: we run the checks (title, fees, taxes) and display the pool's terms clearly before you confirm. While the loan is open, the pool holds your property token as collateral, and you remain the beneficial owner of your property throughout. Fabrica is not the custodian, not the lender, and does not set your interest rate. Fabrica also has no control over whether a property can be used as collateral, or over the terms or amounts that can be borrowed against it. Those are determined by the lending pool.

If you get stuck, open the chat bubble in the corner and we'll help.

passages.title: Who is the lender?
passages.text: Learn more: How the lending pool works (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/lending-pool) · How pool lending launched (https://blog.fabrica.land/instant-loans-with-metastreet)

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.sectionTitle: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text: We want you to know exactly how this works before you ever need it. Here is the full timeline, with no sugarcoating.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text:
We email you reminders 14 days, 5 days, and 1 day before your loan matures, in your property's local timezone. Important: emails can occasionally be marked as spam. Always set your own reminders. Default will occur regardless of any notification issues, and repayment responsibility lies solely with you.

If repaying in full is hard, check your property page for a Refinance option, and watch the reminder emails for an extension offer. Acting before the due date gives you the most options.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text:
There is no grace period. If the loan is not fully repaid by the due date, it defaults. Two things are then true at once:

- You are still the beneficial owner of your property.

- The defaulted loan can now move toward liquidation.

Your property page will show a Defaulted Loan card marked overdue.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text: Before any sale, a formal notice is issued under the UCC (the Uniform Commercial Code, the commercial law that governs secured loans). You then have at least 10 days' notice before the auction can begin. The notice explains your redemption rights and deadlines.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text: After the notice period, the property token is sold at a public auction. How long it runs depends on the lending pool: legacy pools ran 24-hour auctions, and newer pools run 2-week auctions. Bids are placed in USDC, a stablecoin (a digital dollar), with a minimum increase of 2% per bid.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text:
- Before the auction starts, full repayment prevents it. Repay the full outstanding amount, including accrued interest and costs, and the process stops and your property returns to your account. Partial payments do not stop the process. Only full repayment does.

- Once the auction starts, bidding in it is the only way to keep the property. You remain the owner until the auction closes, but when it closes, the winning bidder becomes the new owner. If you want to keep your property at that point, you have to be the winning bidder.

- Surplus comes back to you. If the auction brings in more than your debt plus costs, the excess is returned to you. If it brings in less, you receive nothing, but the property is sold at public auction rather than simply taken by the lender.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What if I can't repay my loan by the due date?
passages.text:
The loan's only recourse is the property token itself. Once the liquidation completes, you owe nothing further, even if the auction brought in less than your debt. Fabrica does not report to credit bureaus, so a default here does not appear on your credit report.

A default might affect your future borrowing on Fabrica, though: your repayment history here can be taken into account when future loan offers are calculated. If your situation is heading this way, talk to us early: open the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Loan defaults in detail (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/loan-defaults)
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What can I do with my property while it's under a loan?
passages.sectionTitle: What can I do with my property while it's under a loan?
passages.text: While a loan is open, your property token is held by the lending pool as collateral. You are still the beneficial owner, but some actions are paused until the loan is repaid. Here is the honest list.

passages.title: What can I do with my property while it's under a loan?
passages.text:
- Transfers between your wallets. The Transfer Property button is disabled and shows: "Please pay off the loan to enable property transfer."

- Removing the property (off-ramp). Remove Property is disabled until the loan is paid off.

- Editing photos and the description. Updating your property page is paused until the loan is repaid.

passages.title: What can I do with my property while it's under a loan?
passages.text:
- Selling. You CAN list your property for sale while it is under a loan. Click Put for sale as usual. The listing form shows your loan payoff math, and your price must at least cover the payoff (you will see a warning if it does not). If the property sells, the sale pays off your loan automatically at closing and you receive the rest. One limit: you can't accept an offer while the loan is open; the offers list says "Pay off your loan to accept an offer."

- Your taxes. Not really an "action", but worth repeating: property taxes remain your responsibility during the loan, and unpaid taxes will block future borrowing.

passages.title: What can I do with my property while it's under a loan?
passages.sectionTitle: The quickest way to unblock everything
passages.text:
Pay off the loan. Use Pay off loan on the Your loan card, and the token returns to your account with all actions restored. See "Repaying your loan" (https://help.fabrica.land/en/articles/16280911-repaying-your-loan) in this collection.

If you get stuck, open the chat bubble in the corner and we'll help.

passages.title: What happens when a loan defaults?
passages.sectionTitle: What happens when a loan defaults?
passages.text: If you provide capital to a lending pool, you should know exactly what happens when a borrower does not repay. Here is the process, step by step.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What happens when a loan defaults?
passages.text:
- Default at maturity. There is no grace period. If a loan is not fully repaid by its due date, it is in default. Borrowers receive reminder emails 14 days, 5 days, and 1 day before maturity.

- UCC notice. Before any sale, a formal disposition notice is issued under the UCC (the Uniform Commercial Code, the law governing secured lending). The borrower gets at least 10 days' notice.

- Public auction. After the notice period, the property token is sold at a public auction. How long it runs depends on the pool: legacy pools ran 24-hour auctions, and newer pools run 2-week auctions. Bids are in USDC, a stablecoin (a digital dollar), with a minimum increase of 2% per bid.

- Recovery. Auction proceeds repay the outstanding debt and costs. Any surplus above that is returned to the borrower.

The borrower can prevent the auction by repaying in full before it starts. Partial payments do not stop the process. Once the auction starts, the borrower keeps the property only by being the winning bidder. In this model the pool does not take the land directly; recovery comes through a public sale, which keeps the process clean and market-priced.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: What happens when a loan defaults?
passages.text: Each property sits in its own trust with a deed recorded at the county, and the property token controls the trust. Transfers of the token to lending contracts are custody only; beneficial ownership stays with the borrower until the collateral is sold at public auction. The collateral interest is designed around UCC Article 12, the commercial-law framework for digital assets. The legal protections for lenders are documented in detail in the developer docs linked below.

passages.title: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.sectionTitle: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.text: Yes. Your ownership isn’t locked to Fabrica. There are three main paths.

passages.title: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.text:
Your Property Token is a standard token on Ethereum (an ERC-1155), so it can be listed on general marketplaces such as OpenSea. A buyer who purchases the token owns the property through its trust.

One important distinction: this applies to genuine sales you agree to. A stolen or otherwise unauthorized transfer does not by itself carry ownership of the property with it. If your token is ever taken without your consent, contact us immediately through the chat bubble and see “What happens if my token is stolen?” (https://help.fabrica.land/en/articles/8848819-what-happens-if-my-token-is-stolen).

Tradeoffs to weigh:

- Those marketplaces aren’t built for real estate, so buyers see far less of the property detail, documents, and history than they would on Fabrica.

- Fabrica’s checkout protections, like the ownership disclosures, the trust-acceptance step, and bank-payment options, only apply on fabrica.land.

passages.title: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.text:
You can market your land anywhere: a local agent, a land listing site, a sign on the road. When you find a buyer, you have two options:

- Close on Fabrica. Send the buyer your property page and they can buy it right on the page, paying by bank account or crypto. This is usually the fastest close.

- Remove the property first. If the buyer wants a conventional closing, remove the property from Fabrica (the off-ramp). A deed is recorded putting title back in your name, and you sell the traditional way. There is no platform fee to remove a property.

passages.title: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.text: Inside the Fabrica app, Transfer Property only moves a property between your own linked and verified wallets. It is not a way to send the token to a buyer. A truly private token sale would happen outside the app, wallet to wallet, and you’d give up Fabrica’s protections for the payment side, so most private deals are better done through the marketplace or an offer.

passages.title: Can I sell my property outside Fabrica?
passages.text:
Fabrica’s marketplace exists so land sells with full information and a safe settlement, where payment and ownership transfer happen together. Selling elsewhere is your right, and always will be, but for most sellers the native marketplace is the simplest and safest route.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Trading (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/trading) and the off-ramp (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/off-ramp) in our docs.

passages.title: What happens to my property if Fabrica disappears?
passages.sectionTitle: What happens to my property if Fabrica disappears?
passages.text: Your property is fine. We designed it that way on purpose.

passages.title: What happens to my property if Fabrica disappears?
passages.sectionTitle: Why your ownership doesn’t depend on us
passages.text:
You own your property through your own trust. You are the beneficiary, and by default you are also your own trustee. Fabrica never holds title to your property and cannot control it. Three things anchor that, none of which need Fabrica to exist:

- Your deed is recorded at the county. The trust’s title to your land sits in the public record, exactly like any other deed.

- The trust stands on its own. Fabrica is not a party to your trust and does not manage it. It keeps working with or without us.

- The trust agreement is open source. Anyone, including your lawyer, can read the full legal text at any time.

passages.title: What happens to my property if Fabrica disappears?
passages.sectionTitle: You could still exit, without us
passages.text: Your Property Token lives on Ethereum, a public network that no company runs. You can retire (“burn”) the token yourself using a public tool like Etherscan, and a real-estate lawyer can complete the deed that puts title directly in your name. No Fabrica website required, no permission needed.

passages.title: What happens to my property if Fabrica disappears?
passages.text:
Honesty matters here: the conveniences would go. The Fabrica website, the marketplace, borrowing through the lending pool, and the services we run around your property could become unavailable or unmaintained. Your ownership, your trust, and your recorded deed would be untouched.

If you want to see how removal works in detail, the Removing your property collection walks through it, or message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Off-ramp (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/off-ramp) · The Fabrica trust is open source (https://blog.fabrica.land/copy-from-us-the-fabrica-trust-is-open-source)

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.sectionTitle: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.text: Owning land through Fabrica is real ownership. That means the property taxes are yours too. This article covers who pays, how to find your bill, and what happens if taxes go unpaid.

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.text:
You do. Whoever owns the property on Fabrica at any given time is responsible for the property taxes, exactly as with any land you own. Fabrica does its best to surface tax information, but paying on time is your responsibility, and Fabrica is not responsible for late or missed payments.

If you buy a property and the previous owner left taxes unpaid, the outstanding balance follows the property. As the new owner, you owe it, and it may be difficult or impossible to recover that money from the seller. Check the tax status before you buy.

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.sectionTitle: How much do I owe, and where do I pay?
passages.text:
Property taxes are set and collected by the county where the land sits. They are usually due once or twice a year, and the amount is based on the county's assessed value of the property.

To find your bill:

- Search the web for your county's name plus "property taxes".

- On the county website, look for the Tax Collector or Treasurer section.

- Look up your property by its APN (the parcel number on your tax bill and on your Fabrica property page).

- You can usually see the amount due, the due dates, and pay online.

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.sectionTitle: Why does the bill show a trust's name instead of mine?
passages.text:
At the county, your property is titled in the name of your own trust. That is how Fabrica ownership works: you are the beneficiary of the trust, and by default you are also your own trustee. Some counties are also slow to update their records after a transfer, so the bill may show the trust or a previous owner's name.

Regardless of the name printed on the bill, the current owner is the one who owes the taxes. If you would like the name or mailing address on file corrected, contact us and we will help.

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.text: County mailing records can lag behind, so a tax bill may go to an old address or arrive late. You still owe the taxes even if no notice reaches you. Check your county's website at least once a year, or set a reminder around your county's due dates.

passages.title: Your property taxes: who pays, how much, and why it matters
passages.sectionTitle: What happens if taxes go unpaid
passages.text:
Unpaid property taxes have real consequences:

- The county can place a lien on the property and eventually sell it at a tax sale.

- Under the trust agreement, a tax sale can trigger automatic dissolution of your trust and void the token. In plain terms: if the county sells the land for unpaid taxes, the Fabrica token no longer represents anything.

- Borrowing on Fabrica is blocked unless your taxes are verifiably current. If the tax status is unknown, that blocks loans too.

- The "Property taxes paid" check in your property's Property checks stops passing, and buyers and lenders can see that on your property page.

Keeping taxes current is the single most important thing you can do as an owner.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: Property obligations (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/property-obligations)

passages.title: Who is Fabrica?
passages.text:
Fabrica serves as a facilitator in real estate transactions, connecting traditional property ownership with blockchain technology.

For its users, Fabrica utilizes blockchain technology to represent property ownership in a digital format. Each property is held in its own trust, which holds record title, and a digital Property Token represents ownership of that trust. Transferring the token transfers ownership of the trust, and with it the property.

For counties, Fabrica streamlines onchain information about the property to give assessors the relevant information they need to do their constitutional duties. When beneficial ownership of a property changes, a change of ownership is reported to the county through the normal channels.

For an overview of Fabrica, the protocol and live properties, see about.fabrica.land (https://about.fabrica.land).

For more detail on how the platform works, see the developer documentation at docs.fabrica.land (https://docs.fabrica.land), including the overview of the regulatory framework (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/regulatory-framework). Questions are always welcome at hello@fabrica.land.

passages.title: What is the Fabrica Trust and how does it affect property transactions?
passages.sectionTitle: What is the Fabrica Trust and how does it affect property transactions?
passages.text:
The Fabrica Trust is a legal structure designed to streamline and digitize property transactions on blockchain. It acts as a bridge between traditional property ownership and onchain representation. Each property sits in its own trust, and that trust holds record title to the property.

Here are some of the key characteristics of the Fabrica Trust:

Tokenization: Once the property is in the trust, a digital token (the Property Token) is minted, which represents ownership of the trust. This token is held directly by the user, signifying control and ownership of the trust, and consequently the property. Transferring the token transfers ownership of the trust.

Nominee Trust: Under the Trust Agreement, the role of trustee is simply as an agent of the beneficiary. The beneficiary is the owner of the property held in the nominee trust, is by default their own trustee, and is ultimately responsible for all property taxes.

Trust Purpose: The purpose of the trust is to allow the beneficiary to use blockchain to manage ownership of a property and facilitate any future transfer of beneficial ownership (at which time a change of ownership will be reported to the county).

The Trust Agreement is open source and governed by California law, while conveyancing follows the law of the state where the property sits. In 2022, California State Board of Equalization tax counsel stated, in an informational analysis for property-tax purposes, that "a transfer of the digital Token is, in substance, a transfer of the underlying real property itself" (California only, and not a legal ruling).

passages.title: What is the Fabrica Trust and how does it affect property transactions?
passages.sectionTitle: What is the Fabrica Trust and how does it affect property transactions?
passages.text: In essence, a Fabrica Trust transforms the traditional property ownership model into a digital, blockchain-compatible format, providing users with flexibility and control over their real estate assets. For the full legal detail, see the Fabrica Trust documentation (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/fabrica-trust).

passages.title: What is Fabrica's role?
passages.text:
Fabrica is a platform, not a title holder. Each property is held in its own trust; the owner is the beneficiary of that trust and, by default, also serves as their own trustee. Fabrica never holds title to a user's property and cannot control it.

What Fabrica builds is the technology around those trusts: the smart contracts and platform that allow users to create and interact with digital property, plus a suite of tools and standardized agreements, including the Fabrica Trust, that bolsters digital property ownership.

While all of this data is publicly available onchain, Fabrica provides convenient access to relevant data about digital property ownership. Fabrica supports county officials in administrative processes related to property records, including recording deeds and reporting changes of ownership. In doing so, Fabrica seeks to enhance accessibility and transparency in real estate transactions.

Fabrica holds 20+ regulatory licenses. Fabrica has operations across all 50 states with varying degrees of functionality. Details are documented at docs.fabrica.land (https://docs.fabrica.land), including licenses and operation (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/licenses-and-operation). For anything else, contact hello@fabrica.land.

passages.title: Can I add multiple properties at once?
passages.sectionTitle: Can I add multiple properties at once?
passages.text: Yes, with one honest caveat: each property goes through its own process. Every parcel gets its own trust, its own deed, its own county recording, and its own fee authorization. There's no shortcut around that, because each one becomes its own recorded piece of paperwork at the county.

passages.title: Can I add multiple properties at once?
passages.sectionTitle: Each parcel stays its own property
passages.text: Every parcel gets its own trust and its own Property Token, and that stays true forever. Parcels cannot be merged into a single token, a single listing, or a single loan. Even adjacent parcels you think of as one piece of land are separate properties on Fabrica: each is listed, sold, and borrowed against on its own.

passages.title: Can I add multiple properties at once?
passages.text: Here's the part that saves you real time: signing can be batched. If you're adding several properties, wait until the documents for all of them are ready. Then you can sign the whole stack in one single online notary session, no matter how many properties you're adding.

passages.title: Can I add multiple properties at once?
passages.text:
If you have many parcels, you don't have to enter them one by one. Email us at hello@fabrica.land with a list of your properties (the APN and county for each) and we'll set up the process for you.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: How adding a property works (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/on-ramp)

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.sectionTitle: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text: Owning land through Fabrica is full ownership: possession, control, the right to sell, lease, or borrow against it, and all the income it produces. Full ownership also means the normal obligations of a landowner stay with you. Fabrica is the platform you own it through, not a property manager.

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text: The big one. Taxes are owed to the county every year, whether or not a bill reaches you. Unpaid taxes can lead to liens, a county tax sale, a blocked loan capacity, and a "Property taxes paid" check that stops passing on your property page. See "Your property taxes" (https://help.fabrica.land/en/articles/8809464-who-pays-property-taxes) in this collection for the full picture.

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text: Counties and local authorities can require upkeep. A common example: in fire-prone areas you may be required to clear brush or keep trees pruned. Weed abatement, fencing, and dumping rules also come up. Notices about these usually come from the county, and mail sent to your property or trust is scanned and emailed to you, so read what arrives and act on it.

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text: If the property sits in an HOA or a road-maintenance association, those dues are yours to pay. Any liens or assessments recorded against the property follow the property, not the previous owner, so keep an eye on them and resolve them where you can.

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text: Fabrica does not insure your land. Whether to carry liability or other coverage is your decision, as it would be with any property you own, and it is worth discussing with an insurance professional, especially if people access the land.

passages.title: What are my responsibilities as a property owner?
passages.text:
If a traditional landowner would have to handle it, you have to handle it. Fabrica gives you the tools to own, sell, and borrow at the speed of software, and forwards you the mail, but the land and its obligations are yours.

Questions about a specific notice or obligation? Message us through the chat bubble in the corner, or email hello@fabrica.land.

Learn more: Property obligations (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/property-obligations)

passages.title: Are Fabrica's smart contracts audited?
passages.text: No. Fabrica’s smart contracts have not been audited by an outside security firm. We would rather tell you that plainly than dress it up.

passages.title: Are Fabrica's smart contracts audited?
passages.sectionTitle: Why your ownership doesn’t hinge on the contracts
passages.text:
Here is the part that matters for you as an owner: Fabrica was designed so that your property does not depend on any piece of software being perfect.

- Your deed is recorded at the county. Title to your land is held by your own trust and sits in the public record, exactly like any other deed. No software bug can erase a county record.

- The trust stands apart from the code. You own your property through your own trust. You are the beneficiary, and by default you are also your own trustee. The trust is a legal structure, not a smart contract, and it survives any technical issue.

- Everything is open. The trust agreement is open source, and the contracts live on Ethereum where anyone can inspect them. You or your advisors can verify what the system does rather than trusting our description of it.

- You can always exit. Removing your property (the off-ramp) puts a fresh deed directly in your name, and it works even without Fabrica.

passages.title: Are Fabrica's smart contracts audited?
passages.text:
We take security seriously and we do not overclaim. If the audit status changes, we will update this article. In the meantime, if you have specific technical questions, message us through the chat bubble in the corner and we will get you a straight answer.

Learn more: The Fabrica protocol (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/protocol) · The Fabrica trust is open source (https://blog.fabrica.land/copy-from-us-the-fabrica-trust-is-open-source)

passages.title: What happens if my token is stolen?
passages.sectionTitle: What happens if my token is stolen?
passages.text: First, take a breath: a stolen token is not the same as stolen land.

passages.title: What happens if my token is stolen?
passages.sectionTitle: Why the thief doesn't become the owner
passages.text:
Your property is owned through a trust, and the trust agreement is explicit: a transfer made without your permission does not carry beneficial ownership with it. The thief may hold the token, but that alone does not make them the owner of your property.

One honest nuance. The law that covers digital assets like these (UCC Article 12) gives certain protections to a later buyer who purchases in good faith with no idea the token was stolen. That means the outcome is not automatic in every case, and it means speed matters: the sooner the theft is on record, the harder it is for anyone to claim they bought innocently.

passages.title: What happens if my token is stolen?
passages.text:
- Contact us immediately. Use the chat bubble at fabrica.land (https://fabrica.land) or email hello@fabrica.land. Include your property link and what happened.

- Report it to law enforcement. A theft report creates the official record that supports any recovery.

- Save everything. Screenshots, emails, anything showing the unauthorized transfer.

Reporting it to us matters right away, not just later. When we confirm a theft report, we flag the token in our systems: a flagged token cannot be sold through the Fabrica marketplace, and it no longer qualifies for a new loan from the lending pool. That closes off the main ways a thief could turn your property into money while the theft is investigated.

Fabrica can provide the onchain transaction history to support an investigation. Because everything on Ethereum is public and permanent, the trail of who moved the token, and when, is there for investigators to see.

passages.title: What happens if my token is stolen?
passages.text:
We cannot reverse an onchain transfer or pull the token back ourselves. Fabrica never holds your token and has no admin keys over it, which is exactly why nobody, including us, can move your property behind your back. Fabrica is not a law firm and cannot give legal advice, so for a contested case, bring in a lawyer. We will cooperate with the facts.

Learn more: UCC Article 12 (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/ucc-article-12) · The Fabrica Trust (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/fabrica-trust)

passages.title: Does Fabrica control my property?
passages.text: No. You own your property through your own trust. You are the beneficiary, and by default you are also your own trustee. Fabrica never holds title to your property and cannot control it.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Does Fabrica control my property?
passages.text:
Each property sits in its own trust, and the trust holds the record title at the county. Your Property Token represents ownership of that trust: transfer the token, and you transfer the property. Fabrica is not a party to your trust. We cannot change it, act for it, or touch the title it holds.

The same is true onchain. There are no admin keys that let Fabrica move your token, take your property, or override your ownership. We cannot transfer your token, and we also cannot reverse a transfer you make, so double-check addresses before sending anything.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Does Fabrica control my property?
passages.sectionTitle: Don't take our word for it
passages.text:
The trust agreement is open source, so you or your lawyer can read exactly what it says. And because your deed is recorded at the county, your ownership is anchored in the public record, not in our database. Everything, including transfer, recovery, and removing the property, works even if Fabrica disappears.

If you have questions about your specific trust, open the Records card on your property page and read the trust agreement there, or message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: The Fabrica Trust (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/fabrica-trust) · The Fabrica trust is open source (https://blog.fabrica.land/copy-from-us-the-fabrica-trust-is-open-source)

passages.title: Who sets the price of a property for sale?
passages.sectionTitle: Who sets the price of a property for sale?
passages.text: You do. When you list a property with Put for sale, you enter the price you want, and buyers can purchase at that price.

passages.title: Who sets the price of a property for sale?
passages.text:
Most property pages show an estimated value. Treat it as a starting point, not an appraisal. It can help you pick a number, but it is not a promise of what your land is worth or what it will sell for.

If you list below the estimated value, the listing flow asks you to check an extra box confirming you understand. That's just a guardrail so nobody underprices by accident.

passages.title: Who sets the price of a property for sale?
passages.text: No. Fabrica is the platform, not a real estate broker, and we don't recommend prices or provide valuations for your sale. If you want a professional opinion, talk to a local appraiser or land agent.

passages.title: Who sets the price of a property for sale?
passages.sectionTitle: What if a buyer thinks the price is off?
passages.text:
Buyers can use Send offer on any property, listed or not. You'll be notified and can accept an offer you like, so the market can meet you in the middle.

If you get stuck, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.

Learn more: how estimated values work (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/property-valuation) in our docs.

passages.title: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.sectionTitle: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.text: Many property pages show an Estimated value. On a property page it sits as a row inside the Marketplace card, right under the asking price when the property is listed. Here is what that number is, where it comes from, and how much weight to give it.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.text:
The estimate is based on third-party data. Click the Estimated value row (View details) and it expands to one line per source, with its value and, where the source reports one, its confidence level, which reflects how much data was available to compute the estimate. You will typically see two kinds of figures:

- Estimated values come from third-party providers whose algorithms estimate market value from comparable prices in the area, adjusted for the size of the property.

- Assessed values come straight from the county tax assessor: the value of the parcel at its latest county assessment.

The headline number is the highest value among the sources, leaving out any source whose confidence is under 50%. A source below that line stays in the list, marked "Not used". County assessed values carry no confidence figure, so they always count, and a property's last sale price is listed but never used as the headline. When no source qualifies, the row shows "Not available". When the number that leads is the county's figure, the row is labeled Tax-assessed value instead of Estimated value.

Where a detailed report is available, the expanded row also offers a Download valuation report link, so you can save the full breakdown for your own records.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.sectionTitle: Why the county's assessed value looks so different
passages.text:
It is common for the two groups to diverge a lot. Assessed values are set for property-tax purposes, not to track the market. Counties often update them infrequently, and for land they commonly sit far below what parcels actually trade for. Algorithmic estimates try to track the market but work with limited data, especially for rural land where comparable sales are scarce. In some states, sale prices are not even public record, so the data behind any land estimate is structurally thin.

That is why the assessed value, market listings, and estimates can all disagree about the same parcel. None of them is "the" price. Treat every number, ours included, as a starting point.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.sectionTitle: Why don't I see an estimated value?
passages.text:
Not every property page shows an estimate. The estimate depends on third-party data, and whether a value appears can differ from property to property. On a property listed for sale, the price that matters is the one the seller has set.

If you don't see an estimate, that says nothing about what the property is worth. You can always research the area yourself, and buyers can send an offer at whatever price they think is right. If you have a question about a specific property, message us through the chat bubble in the corner.
passages.updatedAt: updated a week ago at build

passages.title: Where does the estimated value come from?
passages.sectionTitle: A starting point, not an appraisal
passages.text:
Treat the estimated value as a starting point, not an appraisal. As the page itself puts it, "These values are a starting point, not an appraisal." It is one signal among many, not a promise of what the property is worth or what it would sell for. Fabrica is not a real-estate broker and does not advise on pricing. If you need a defensible number, talk to a licensed appraiser, and always do your own diligence on location, access, and features before buying or setting a price.

Learn more: Property valuation (https://docs.fabrica.land/docs/property-valuation)
